title: Faithful and modest
hookLine: you help your city not by holding office but by being trustworthy and self-respecting (Enchiridion 24)

lines: THE NEIGHBOR WHO SIGNS FOR PACKAGES.
cards: Down the hall lives the neighbor who signs for your packages and actually remembers to tell you. Who returns the ladder. Who says she'll water the plants while you're away, and you come home to plants that are alive.
She doesn't sit on the city council. She'll never have a plaque. But the whole building runs a little better because she's in it.

Section twenty-four of the handbook imagines a student who worries that a philosopher with no money and no office is useless to his friends and his city. Epictetus answers, and that neighbor is in the answer.

teach.b: Don't let thoughts like this trouble you, Epictetus says: I'll live without honor, a nobody everywhere. Getting an office, being invited to a dinner, those aren't up to you. So how can missing them be your dishonor?
You only need to be somebody in what's yours, and there you can be worth a great deal. But my friends will get no help from me, the student says. What help?
Who told you those were in your power? Show me how to get them while staying trustworthy and self-respecting and generous, and I'll get them.
But if you ask me to lose my own good so you can have things that aren't truly good, see how unfair that is.
And which would you rather have: money, or a faithful, self-respecting friend? But my country will get no help from me. What help?

teach.h: NO BATHS FROM YOU, AND THAT'S FINE.
teach.b: It won't get colonnades or public baths from you. Fine. It doesn't get shoes from the blacksmith either, or weapons from the shoemaker.
It's enough if each does their own work. If you made one more citizen trustworthy and self-respecting, would that be no use?
Faithful is pistos: trustworthy, the one whose word holds. Modest is aidemon: self-respecting, with a sense of shame in the good sense, the person who won't do what's beneath them.
What place will you hold in the city, then?
Whatever place you can hold while staying faithful and modest. Lose those trying to help, he says, and what use will you be, faithless and shameless?

how: Some Stoic practitioners measure their usefulness less by status or money than by being trustworthy and self-respecting in ordinary dealings.

o: a generous donor who builds a city's baths
a well-known public official honored with a plaque
faithful: trustworthy, the one whose word holds

games.q: faithful and modest — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says a philosopher without office is useless to the city
one more trustworthy, self-respecting citizen is real help.
he says getting invited to a dinner isn't up to you
so missing it can't be your dishonor.
he says to give up your honesty if it helps your friends get money
losing your own good for things that aren't good is unfair, he says.

games.q: a student says: without office or money, I can't help my country. what does Epictetus answer?
o: if you made one more citizen faithful and modest, is that no use?
you're right; withdraw from the city.
games.why: it's enough if each does their own work; a trustworthy, self-respecting citizen is real help.

practice: Think of one small promise that's still open, returning something, answering a message, showing up when you said, and picture keeping it simply, without fuss. Notice how small it is, and how much it says.
Let the words settle with the breath: faithful on the in breath, modest on the out.

wordCard.voice: Pistos. The Greek word for faithful, trustworthy, the one whose word holds; Epictetus' answer to feeling useless: you already serve your friends and your city. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 24: faithful and modest, trustworthy and self-respecting.

carryVoice: Your line: each does their own work. A word that holds is no small use. Until tomorrow.
